reviews.title: Events Tab
reviews.text:
I am extremely disappointed with the replacement of Tinder’s original Explore categories with the new Events tab.

The original categories were genuinely useful because they allowed users to find people based on what they were looking for, whether that was a serious relationship, friendship, something casual, or verified profiles.

reviews.title: Misleading advertising and inconsistent subscription benefits
reviews.text:
Misleading advertising and inconsistent subscription benefits

I purchased Tinder Gold for £15, expecting to receive the advertised benefits, including one free Boost per month. However, no free Boost was provided, and the app is asking me to pay an additional £8 to use one, despite having just paid for a Gold subscription.

After researching the issue, I discovered that some Gold subscribers may not receive the monthly Boost. If this is the case, I believe this should be made absolutely clear before customers pay for their subscription.

It is unacceptable for customers to pay for a premium service without clear information about which advertised benefits they will actually receive. This raises serious concerns about transparency and potentially misleading advertising.

I am extremely disappointed with this experience and will be raising a formal complaint and reporting my concerns to Trading Standards.

Customers deserve clear, honest advertising and transparency about what they are paying for.

reviews.title: Tinder’s distance settings are not working — a serious privacy and security concern
reviews.text:
I have my Discovery settings set to a maximum distance of 50 km, and I have the Global option switched OFF. Despite this, I am still being connected with people from all over the world.

The whole point of having distance limits and the option to turn off Global is to control who you see and who can see your profile. I do not want to receive messages from people on the other side of the world, and I do not want my profile being shown to people who live thousands of kilometres away.

This is not just an inconvenience; it is a serious privacy and security concern. My photos and personal information are being exposed to people in countries where online scams and identity theft are significant concerns. This creates an unnecessary risk for users who have specifically chosen to limit their visibility.

If I have selected a 50 km radius and disabled Global, Tinder should respect those settings. Users should be able to trust that their profiles are not being shown worldwide against their stated preferences.

Tinder needs to fix this issue urgently. Distance and discovery settings should work as advertised, and users deserve proper control over their privacy, visibility and personal information.

I lasted about five minutes: I’ve never downloaded a betting app, but Tinder felt as close to one as I’ll ever get. The UX was crowded and awful, difficult to navigate, and looked like it was screaming out for money. Actually reading a profile seemed completely secondary, as if knowing about the person doesn’t matter anymore.

Incredibly sad to see where dating apps/Tinder is in 2026, but glad to have had so many great times from this app between 2017 and 2019: back when you could get three boosts for ~£6.00, a Gold subscription for ~£12.00 a month, and ~1 date per week, as a straight, tall, dark and handsome guy in East London, if you wanted it.

Glory days, never to return…

reviews.title: Tinder should keep Premium features, but basic matching should remain free.
reviews.text:
If two people mutually like each other, they should be able to match and start a conversation without either person having to purchase Tinder Premium. Free users should also receive a reasonable daily number of likes/swipes so they have a genuine opportunity to make connections.

When Tinder shows a user that someone has liked their profile but hides that person’s identity behind a paywall, it can create pressure to purchase Premium just to find out who is interested. Tinder should be more transparent about how these likes and notifications work and give free users a genuine opportunity to make mutual matches.

Premium should provide additional features and convenience, rather than being necessary for basic human connection.

I hope Tinder considers introducing a fairer free matching system where genuine mutual matches can communicate without requiring a paid subscription.

While Tinder uses face scanning ("Face Check") to protect users from catfish and bots, the practice introduces significant cybersecurity, privacy, and legal risks. Cybersecurity and legal experts outline several critical concerns with giving biometric data to a dating app:

1. Permanence of Biometric Data (No "Reset" Button)If a hacker steals your password, you can change it. You cannot change your face. If a database breach occurs or the encrypted mathematical representations of your face—your "FaceMap" or "FaceVector"—are leaked, that biometric identity is permanently compromised. Operators expanding biometric checks must evaluate this lifelong legal and identity theft exposure.

Under Match Group’s privacy policies, this data can be shared with parent company affiliates, service providers, and vendors. reviews.title: Paid More, Matched Less
reviews.text:
I’ve downloaded Tinder more times than I can count, and unfortunately I’ve never had a meaningful experience with it. From my perspective, the app feels heavily driven by its algorithm rather than by helping people make genuine connections.

The app frequently tells me that several people have already liked my profile, yet after spending time swiping, I rarely end up with a single match. The most frustrating part is the premium subscription. You would expect that paying for unlimited likes and additional visibility would improve your chances of matching, but in my experience, it made no difference at all. In fact, it almost seemed like I received fewer matches while I was subscribed. Strangely enough, after my subscription expired, I started receiving matches again.

Of course, this is only my personal experience, but after trying the app multiple times over the years, I can’t justify recommending it. If you’re looking for a genuine relationship, I don’t believe Tinder is the right place to find one.

reviews.title: Better off Single than with this scam of an app!
reviews.text:
In a moment when the U.S. is loudly debating inclusion and basic dignity for trans and gender-nonconforming people, this app is a bleak reminder of how far we still have to go. Despite being fully verified and completely transparent on my profile, I was repeatedly reported as “fake” and blocked—simply because too many straight men can’t be bothered to read a profile before reacting. Instead of swiping left, they hit “report,” and the app lets their ignorance dictate the experience.

What takes this from disappointing to outrageous is that I was a premium member. I paid for a week-long subscription, and the app kept my profile “pending verification” for the entire paid period. No access, no visibility, no communication, no support team to contact—nothing. They took the money and delivered absolutely zero service. How is that not, at minimum, a violation of the spirit of Apple’s App Store standards? At the very least, it raises serious questions about consumer protection when an app can charge users, lock them out, and refuse any refund or credit.

This platform could have been a space for genuine conversation, but instead it mirrors the broader climate in America right now: marginalized people get pushed aside while companies cater to the comfort and complaints of the majority. It’s time for apps like this to be held accountable—for their policies, their silence, and the money they take while offering nothing in return.
